People with disability.
rationale:
Conflict escalation between Ukraine and Russia is still expected as initially raised. The low-level conflict in east Ukraine continues, while political tensions and military movements between Russia and Ukraine increased at the end of March 2021, when an estimated 100,000–150,000 Russian troops moved to the western border of Ukraine. Although Russia removed parts of the troops by mid-May, Ukraine and Russia raised mutual accusations of military preparedness activities. (Al Jazeera 19/04/2021, 21/04/2021, 22/04/2021, and 11/05/2021; EU 12/04/2021; Kyivpost 12/06/2021).
Military preparations continued from both sides in the following month, including the increased Russian forces presence ate the border with Ukraine (also from the Belarus side of the border). The number and scale of the deployed military is likely capable of a full-scale operation in Ukraine.  (BBC 15/11/2021, The Washington Post 30/10/2021) (Sky News 18/12/2021, )


The number of ceasefire violations have increased by at least 64% in Q4 of 2021 (till 19 Dec), compared to Q3. Over 34,600 violations were reported in Q4 compared with over 21,000 violations in the third quarter of 2021 including the use of heavy weapon. (OSCE accessed 23/12/2021, OSCE accessed 23/12/2021)


In the event of materialization of the risk, civilian casualties, displacement, acute humanitarian needs, damage to infrastructure, and increased access constraints. The scale and intensity of the impact depend on the scale of the conflict (NPR 07/12/2021, OCHA 30/11/2021, Crisisgroup 08/12/2021, OCHA 02/12/2021)

risk_title: An increasing number of migrants on the Belarusian-Polish borders and continued access restrictions result in increased humanitarian needs for the displaced.
trigger: National migration policies not open to high numbers of migrants arrivals; political tensions between Belarus and the EU; harsh winter conditions; COVID-19 measures
vulnerability: Migrants
rationale: Migrants and asylum seekers are in critical need of shelter and NFIs, protection and legal assistance, medical care, food, and water. They urgently need adequate shelter as winter has begun. The first snow has fallen, and the temperature drops below zero during the night. The border area has harsh winters with extremely cold temperatures and heavy snowfall. • Access to the affected population is constrained on both sides of the border. In September, Polish authorities imposed a state of emergency on 183 localities within 3km of the border with Belarus, blocking humanitarian organisations from accessing the affected population. Grassroots movements and community members are leading the humanitarian response in areas outside state of emergency zones. On the Belarus side, the 3km area closest to the border is only accessible to military and security officials (HRW 24/11/2021). Humanitarian access is sporadic and controlled by authorities.

risk_title: The implementation of the Migrant Protection Protocol leads to an increased number of migrants stranded at the border lacking protection, shelter, and services.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
- Implementation and resumption of the MPP (Migrant Protection Protocols) from 06/12/2021. 
- Return of asylum seekers, who are in the US awaiting processing, to Mexico's borders. 
- Increase in the number of migrants at the border from Mexico to the US, due to the convergence of Title 42 and MPP policies: the former does not allow passage to the US; the latter returns asylum seekers from the US to Mexico.
vulnerability: Around 192,000 law enforcement encounters with migrants have been recorded at the US-Mexico border this year, according to CBP. In cities such as Tijuana, Texas and Ciudad Juarez, shelter capacity has reached up to 70% of capacity. The MPP empowers US authorities to return asylum seekers who are already on US territory, which creates a risk for the authorities' response in terms of shelter, NFI, food security and livelihoods. The northern border has a strong presence of drug cartels and mafias, which puts at risk the sectoral need for protection of the migrant population.
rationale:
The Migrant Protection Protocol (MPP) in the United States will be back in force from Monday 6 December. Through this programme, initially implemented by Trump's administration, the aim is for migrants to wait in Mexican border cities while asylum applications to the United States are processed. This policy works alongside Title 42, which means that, in addition to preventing asylum seekers from passing through, the US government will be able to return asylum seekers already in the US to Mexico's borders. 
This represents a risk for the migrant population, due to the high levels of xenophobia at the borders. In addition, the Protocol would increase the number of migrants at Mexico's borders, where most shelters are almost at capacity (as is the case in Tamaulipas and Reynosa). There is also a risk to the sectoral needs of the migrant population, as many of the border cities are heavily controlled by drug cartels. To date, 1,544 assaults against MPP asylum seekers have been recorded. Legal representation for MPP asylum seekers is limited (only 10% have access).

risk_title: There is a risk of the resurgence of armed clashes in Catatumbo region.
trigger:
- FARC frontline dissidents have begun disputing territories for drug production and trafficking.
- Catatumbo is one of the regions with the highest coca leaf production in Colombia, with around 40,000 hectares. 
- Catatumbo is currently home to the ELN, EPL and the Rastrojos, who a few years ago agreed to a ceasefire and the distribution of illicit activities. 
- The arrival of FARC dissidents in the region could lead to armed confrontations with other groups in the region and cause a resurgence of the armed conflict.
vulnerability: Before the Peace Agreement, Catatumbo was one of the regions where the municipalities that comprise it had a strong presence of armed confrontations, leaving 105,678 victims of forced displacement between 2000 and 2012. Due to the dynamics of the past, some mass displacements tend to be between 2,000 and 5,000 people, which means that the annual figure could be close to 20,000 people affected by forced displacement events. The dispute over this territory is based on the control of illicit crops and drug trafficking routes. Collective and selective assassinations, forced recruitment, displacement, confinement and forced disappearance were frequent in the region. The arrival of FARC-EP dissidents in the territory has led to a resurgence of threats (such as the use of explosive devices) and communiqués that generate tension with the ELN and other groups already controlling the region.
rationale: The territorial division between the armed groups ELN, Los Rastrojos and the EPL made a few years ago has become tense due to the arrival of FARC dissident fronts. The dispute over territorial control has already led to threats of explosives and harassment, and it is expected that the situation could escalate to the levels of the current armed confrontations in Arauca. Catatumbo is one of the regions with the largest area under coca cultivation (40,000 hectares), which makes it a disputed territory between armed groups.

risk_title: Social instability in Nile River state and Northern state over electricity prices results in an increase in food needs.
trigger:
Farmers of the north escalating demands
Clashes between protesters and security forces
Cutting off Khartoum from electricity supply line generated by Merowe Dam
vulnerability: The affected population can meet their food needs by applying, temporarily, some coping strategies, such as reduce the consumption of some nutritious foods. Presence of NGOs in Sudan will likely reduce the impact of the crisis on people.
rationale:
Rationale: In case the blocking continues, it will likely have a negative impact on the agricultural and industrial sectors. Needs for food will likely increase because farmers who depend on electricity for irrigation are warning that their crops (especially wheat) are about to fail. Restricting trucks movement will likely result in an increase in prices of certain items in the markets. In case the farmers’ demands are not met, they are threatening to cut off Khartoum from electricity supply line generated by Merowe Dam, which will likely affect the industrial sector and increase the risk of insecurity in the capital (especially with the political and social instability taking place now). 

Update: In mid-February, the government and farmers reached to an agreement to freeze the increase on electricity prices until 30 April. As at 15 May, no further blockade or impact of the risk is reported.

Context: Shiryan El Shamal (The North Lifeline) highway has been blocked since 9 January by farmers in Ed Debba locality (northern Sudan), who are protesting a 100% surge in electricity prices announced a week earlier by the government. The highway connects Sudan and Egypt, and any truck traffic has been banned by the farmers. As at 12 January, more than 600 Sudanese trucks and 15 Egyptian trucks have been stuck on the highway. 
Despite the “government” announcing a freeze on electricity prices in the agricultural, industrial, and residential sectors on 12 January, the farmers have escalated the civil disobedience until all demands are met. Their demands are cancelling the increase on electricity prices, cancelling the “Northern Path” decision in the Juba agreement, granting the northern region 2% of the electricity produced by the Merowe Dam, and other demands related to development projects. 

FYI
“Northern Path” decision: dividing the income from the proceeds of natural resources, extracted wealth, tax income, other levies and taxes imposed in the region, provided that revenue is split 30%/70% between the Northern Territory government and the central government in Khartoum, valid for ten years.

Merowe Dam: Over 50,000 people were displaced when the dam was built in 2006. The unequal access to electricity from the Merowe Dam in Northern State has been a controversial issue for years and many demonstrations have taken place to demand 2% of its electricity, an investigation into the 2006 killing, compensation for damage caused by the dam’s construction, and an investigation into corruption surrounding the dam.

2006 killings: a clash between government militias and civilians protesting the construction of the Dam resulted in many killings and injuries among residents of the northern states.

risk_title: Worsening drought conditions increase humanitarian needs in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Somalia.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
-Somalia, Kenya and Ethiopia have experienced four consecutive below average rainy seasons
-Weather forecasts indicate possibility of a fifth consecutive below average rainy season during the Oct-Dec 2022 rainy season
vulnerability: Drought-affected communities have experienced several shocks within the past 5 years. They have high poverty levels and have faced protracted conflict and recurrent natural hazards.
rationale:
Drought conditions in Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia have been steadily worsening since 2021. The 2022 March-May rainy season was the fourth consecutive below average rainy season. This has contributed to an increase in the number of people facing food insecurity, from 12 to 14 million people in first quarter of 2022 to 15 to 16 million in the second quarter. In Somalia, some areas like Baidoa district(Bay region) are facing Famine (IPC Phase 5) food security conditions, with high mortality rates.
Weather forecasts are indicating a significant likelihood that the October to December 2022 rainy season will also be below average, which would result in a five-season drought. This would further worsen food insecurity in 2023, increasing the number of people requiring humanitarian food assistance and the severity of needs.

risk_title: Economic sanctions lead to the loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity.
trigger: ECOWAS sanctions; lack of liquidities,; inflation
vulnerability: 1.2 million people are already facing a food crisis. The sanctions will further reduce their ability to access to food.
rationale:
On 9 January 2022 the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) decided to apply several economic sanctions against Mali, including the closure of land and air borders with member countries, the suspension of all commercial and financial transactions between ECOWAS countries and Mali, and the freezing of Malian assets in the Central Banks of ECOWAS (ECOWAS 09/01/2022). These sanctions were applied in reaction to the decision of the Transition authorities to postpone the presidential election, initially scheduled for February 2022, and following the submission of a timetable for a transition period of five years at the end of the Assises Nationales de la Refondation −consultations with the population with the objective to fix the date of the next elections and to guarantee the return of civilians to power (TV5Monde 30/12/2021). The five-year period was judged too long by ECOWAS.  These sanctions are likely to cause loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity, aggravated by the persistent conflict and the economic consequences of COVID-19, including difficulties in the supply of food products and agricultural inputs, rising prices, and job losses (IRC 19/01/2022). Even though the authorities try to resort to other neighboring non-ECOWAS countries to circumvent the effects of the sanctions, the transport of essential goods that are exempt from the sanctions will likely be disrupted due to the increase in border controls by neighbouring countries (Le Point 14/01/2022). Border closure with neighboring countries such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire will primarily affect the cotton and gold sectors, which are Mali's main export products (The Guardian 28/01/2022; African Business 14/01/2022; Jeune Afrique 31/01/2022). The decrease in customs revenue due to the reduction in imports while the country can no longer borrow money from regional financial institutions could lead to a lack of cash once the state reserves are exhausted. The salaries of civil servants and the military may therefore not be paid in the coming months (Le Point 14/01/2022). As during the 2020 sanctions, remittances, on which many households depend for their survival are likely to become impossible due to the lack of cash (Le Monde 25/09/2020). Capping withdrawals and stopping the granting of new credit will greatly reduce the coping capacity of those affected (DW 24/09/2020).  

Update 17/10/2022
This risk has partially materialised. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) economic sanctions against Mali were lifted on 3 July 2022 after the junta presented a timetable for the next presidential elections, which it set for March 2024. The individual sanctions against the leaders of the junta and the suspension of Mali from the organs of ECOWAS remain until the return of civilian power in the country. This risk has partially materialised in terms of rising food prices, but the impact of sanctions on humanitarian access has been very limited. The same can be said for the impact of sanctions on livestock farming. The increase in food insecurity has materialised, but food security was expected to deteriorate nationwide regardless of the sanctions, making it difficult to attribute solely to the economic sanctions that lasted almost six months. The decline in trade flows with external markets in connection with ECOWAS sanctions has increased food prices, which continue to be high. Poor households have seen their access to food deteriorate further.

risk_title: The current political crisis is evolving into a countrywide intrastate conflict that will lead to increased large-scale displacement and deterioration of the complex humanitarian crisis.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
- The trial of deposed leader Aung San Suu Kyi likely leading to Increased political tensions and clashes. 
- The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) publicly voicing its support for and alignment with the National Unity Government (NUG). 
- The KIA encouraging all ethnic armed organisations (EAOs) to cooperate in order to resist and “annihilate” the junta under the National Unity Government. 
- The junta's will to dismantle six police departments and absorb the police officers into the military against the anti-coup resistance movement.
- Myanmar junta vowed to intensify action against homegrown militia groups fighting the military-run government, saying the armed forces would “annihilate” them.
- During the military parade, Gen Min Aung Hlaing made a statement about his intent to 'annihilate' armed groups that are fighting against the junta.
vulnerability: Ethnic minorities in areas of active conflict. Politicians, activists, protestors at high risk of being a target.
rationale:
The spread of clashes to more regions between the military and armed resistance is stemming from political tensions and the ongoing emergency state enforced by the junta since the military coup in Feb 2021. There are ongoing clashes between the military and the People's Defense Forces and other ethnic armed groups in the southeast and the northwest, where previously there were none. IDP numbers have been gradually increasing since the coup. Since clashes between the military and anti-coup People's Defense forces supported by some ethnic armed groups first escalated in May 2021, post coup IDP numbers peaked at around 220,000 between June-October 2021, however after October 2021, IDP numbers have more than doubled to over 500,000 IDPs by end of Feb 2022. This is a direct result of the increasingly conflict in Myanmar where disproportional and indiscriminate violence is used against civilians by the military in response to ongoing armed resistance. IDP numbers continue to rise with almost 558,000 IDP as at 28 March.

Intense fighting has been occurring throughout the months of April and May 2022, especially in the north-west regions of Chin, Magway, and Sagaing (UNHCR 06/06/2022a). As of 06 June 2022, the number of IDPs reached a figure of 704,400 and the total number of IDPs in the country crossed the 1 million figure (UNHCR 06/06/2022b).

risk_title: Political violence and attacks by armed groups in Mindanao around the May presidential elections result in displacement and protection issues.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
-electoral period started 
-past episodes of electoral violence in the country 
-candidacy of controversial candidate Ferdinand Marcos Jr  
-presence of armed groups refusing peace talks
vulnerability: IDPs in Mindanao affected by clashes between the security forces and armed groups. Politicians and voters affected by political violence
rationale:
Electoral violence across the Philippines is a threat for the current three-month long election season that started on 8 February. Voters will choose the next president, vice president, and 18,000 other political positions on 9 May (The Diplomat 07/02/2022). Electoral violence by privately hired armed groups include voter intimidation, attacks on polls, and assassination of political rivals (Benar News 02/02/2022 ; New Mandala 08/07/2021 ; PNA 09/02/2022 ; University of Portsmouth 30/09/2021 and  08/10/2021 ; Rappler 14/02/2022; Inquirer 01/12/2021).    

The leading candidate is Ferdinand Marcos Jr., son of Ferdinand Marcos, who held the presidency from 1965 until he was ousted in a people’s revolution in 1986 (Aljazeera 14/12/2022 ; VOA 06/01/2022). In southern Mindanao, Marcos’ policies contributed to land grabs, human rights abuses, and conflict (Inquirer 28/12/2016; Asia Society 08/03/2022). The controversial Marcos Jr.’s candidacy will likely contribute to increased political tensions and violence in Mindanao.   

Mindanao is still affected by ongoing armed group attacks and their clashes with the military. Armed groups, including the New People’s Army (NPA), Maute, Abu Sayyaf, and Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters all refuse peace talks and negotiations with the government, and seek independence from the Philippines (Global Initiative 20/02/2020).  These armed groups may conduct more attacks than usual, taking advantage of the political tensions and authorities’ focus on the elections. Security forces are already being deployed to areas of security concerns across the country, most of which are in Mindanao (Business Mirror 14/02/2022).   

Intercommunal violence in the form of clan feuds including over land disputes also affects Mindanao and causes displacement. Conflict and violence in Mindanao are exacerbated by a shadow economy that provides economic and political means for the groups involved (Global Initiative 20/02/2020; International Alert 04/2014). Mindanao is therefore at a high risk of increased violence and armed groups attacks, including electoral violence by ‘private’ armed groups hired to attack polls and political candidates by rivaling politicians (Benar News 30/06/2021; PhilStar 15/02/2022; Philippine Army 13/01/2022). Polls situated in areas with armed groups presence, particularly the NPA, are most at risk (New Mandala 08/07/2021; Manila Bulletin 13/02/2022).   

In the months preceding the election in the month of May, especially in April, there was a rise in armed conflict in the region, leading to increase in displacements (Protection Cluster accessed 13/06/2022).

risk_title: The detection of COVID-19 cases causes the Government to (re-)enact strict border controls that aggravate food insecurity, resulting in lower food consumption and nutritional diversity levels among the most vulnerable.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger: Jilin province in China bordering the DPRK is affected by a COVID-19 surge (Omicron variant). Although the DPRK has recently resumed limited trade with China, and despite long quarantine measures, disinfection, and testing, DPRK may react to the latest COVID-19 outbreak in China by re-introducing strict border closures.
vulnerability: All DPRK citizens are affected by the complex crisis and COVID-19 measures. People who are already food insecure (40% of the population), particularly vulnerable children, and elderly at risk of starvation.
rationale:
The DPRK is chronically food insecure because its mountainous terrain and climate do not support effective agriculture. In addition, the DPRK is reliant on trade with China and humanitarian aid to cover its food shortages, even though it maintains an official ideology based on economic self-reliance. At least 10 million people were in need of humanitarian aid including food assistance in 2020. Since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, the DPRK has maintained a zero COVID-19 policy, and applied strict measures to contain the potential spread of COVID-19, including border closures since Jan 2020, resulting in shortages in basic supplies including medicines. Food insecurity is exacerbated because of ongoing severe COVID-19 containment measures that have already affected the overall access, humanitarian response, and trade. The government acknowledges economic hardship and food shortages because of the pandemic but it remains reliant on border closures instead of vaccinations. The DPRK has not accepted any vaccinations.

The DPRK already has confirmed its first COVID case in May 2022 which was followed by a strict national lockdown. As of 13 June 2022, around 4.5 million (17% of its total population) suspected COVID cases were reported. The new restrictions is believed to have affected the already dire food insecurity  and nutritional deficiency levels, especially  among the most vulnerable .

risk_title: Electoral violence and increased intercommunal conflict throughout Kenya result in displacement, the disruption of livelihoods, and protection concerns.
trigger: Early expectations of electoral malpractice; Disputed election results after the elections happen in August; Losing candidate refuses to concede; speeches inciting violence by some politicians
vulnerability: The entire Kenyan population is facing an unfavorable economic environment due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, high cost of living/rising inflation and high national debt levels. Some communities in arid/semi-arid counties are using negative coping mechanisms to survive the ongoing drought.
rationale:
Kenya has experienced electoral violence during past elections. There is a likelihood of electoral violence before/during the August 2022 election period. There is currently high political tension, worsened by hate speech by some politicians. The tone of the media is also quite divisive and disinformation campaigns on social media are becoming more frequent. Politicians could also weaponise ongoing resource-based conflicts for their own political gains. 
There is a possibility of displacement of 150,000 people due to localised violence and intercommunal conflicts. Access constraints are also likely to increase in drought affected areas due to intercommunal conflicts.
In 2022, more than 1,060 political disorder events were reported as at 5 August-the highest since 1997. Many of these events happened during party primaries from March to April.
General elections held on 9 August had relatively low voter turnout(65.4%), allegations of voter bribery and technology failures. Even though a petition challenging the presidential election results was rejected by the Supreme Court, there was peace countrywide until William Ruto was inaugurated as President on 13 September.

risk_title: The resurgence of the March 23 Movement (M23) and intensification of conflict lead to displacement and the further deterioration of the humanitarian situation in Nord-Kivu.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger: Nairobi agreements; 2023 presidential election; general insecurity; resurgence of M23 activity.
vulnerability: In Nord Kivu province where dozens of armed groups are active, the increase of M23 attacks will considerably worsen the humanitarian situation, mainly in the territory of Rutshuru where thousands of IDPs and returnees are reported
rationale: The DRC update below refers to the risk initially raised in March 2022 and then updated in the Global Risk Analysis of October 2022. This risk has materialised, while the humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate. Clashes between the Congolese army and the M23 are still continuing, forcing thousands of people to flee. The M23 continues to expand its area of influence and threatens to cut off the main supply routes to Goma, the capital of North Kivu. The killing of more than a hundred people in December 2022 is also attributed to the M23. As at January 2023, more than 520,000 had been displaced since the clashes intensified in March 2022. A lack of food and the poor living conditions of the displaced people in sites in Kanyaruchinya and surrounding areas in Nyiragongo territory led to the declaration of a cholera outbreak by the provincial authorities on 14 December 2022. The confirmed cases have risen to 4,530, with 16 related deaths recorded in Nyiragongo and Karisimbi health zones as at 8 February 2023. The ceasefire agreement concluded in Luanda between the DRC and Rwanda in November 2022, which requires the withdrawal of M23 fighters from areas under their control, has not been followed. In November 2022, East African states deployed a regional force to end armed group violence in eastern DRC. That said, some civil society organisations and inhabitants of North Kivu do not perceive this force as offensive enough. Demonstrations have taken place mainly in Goma to demand the departure of this force or a more offensive attitude towards the M23. The negotiations conducted by the regional force with the M23, perceived by some as support for the armed group, have reinforced doubts on the agenda of the regional force.  The M23 continues to illegally tax people in areas under their control and to forcibly recruit civilians into their ranks.

risk_title: Colombian armed groups in Venezuelan territory change the dynamics towards cross-border non-international armed conflict, leading to an increase in internally displaced Colombians and Venezuelan migrants in Colombia in need of assistance.
trigger:
- Continuation Government disputes (Col-Ven)
- Lack of state presence at the Colombian-Venezuelan border
- Clashes between FARC-EP, ELN, Colombian-Venezuelan hybrid groups, and the Venezuelan Armed Forces increasing
- Increase territorial disputes in border towns between Colombian non-state armed groups
- Search for control of Venezuelan territory by organised armed groups, residual armed groups and organised criminal groups
- Changing dynamics between the Colombian armed groups and the Venezuelan government
vulnerability: The number of people affected corresponds to the approximation of the population located in border cities in Colombia and Venezuela. The lack of response capacity of both states, confinements and threats diminishes the response capacity of humanitarian organisations.
rationale:
The FARC-EP's demobilisation and subsequent withdrawal from the Colombian-Venezuelan border, which followed the 2016 peace agreement, led to the strengthening ELN's control in these areas of Norte de Santander, Arauca, Cesar, La Guajira and Vichada (Colombian border), and Apure, Táchira, Zulia and Amazonas (Venezuelan Border). Moreover, this process opened the way for the formation of armed groups made up of FARC-EP dissidents such as the 10th Front and La Segunda Marquetalia. (InsightCrime 19/10/2021; InsightCrime11/01/2022). 
The armed conflict has begun to deepen since 2020, because armed groups used restrictions on population mobility, as part of COVID-19 confinement measures, to increase their activity, and FARC-EP dissidents began to strengthen and dispute territories on the Colombian-Venezuelan border (departments of Arauca, Norte de Santander and Casanare) with the ELN (InsightCrime11/01/2022). Until the beginning of 2022, the ELN and FARC-EP dissidents had a non-aggression and territorial division agreement that has been broken due to the assassination of some FARC-EP dissident leaders allegedly by ELN forces (Insight Crime 18/01/2022; Ideas Paz 24/01/2022). FARC-EP dissidents begun disputing territories held by the ELN, La Segunda Marquetalia and other armed groups, mainly in Apure, aiming to expand into Venezuela (Insightcrime 13/10/2021). The decrease in illegal rents during 2020 for non-state armed groups in Colombia, due to COVID-19 restrictions that hinder drug trafficking, began to motivate expansion towards Venezuelan territory in search of new illegal economy opportunities.   
Since 2021, clashes between FARC-EP, ELN, Colombian-Venezuelan hybrid groups, and the Venezuelan Armed Forces have begun to increase (InsightCrime11/01/2022; La Opinión 29/04/2021). The ELN's presence in Venezuela for more than 30 years was focused on alliances with the Venezuelan government, drug trafficking and the development of irregular economies (BBC News  04/01/2022; Insightcrime 13/10/2021). However, the arrival and strengthening of FARC dissidents have led to a change in the dynamics of the presence of Colombian non-state armed groups in Venezuela and their relationship with Venezuelan armed groups, giving rise to a Non-International Cross-Border Armed Conflict.  This type of conflict is characterised by the outbreak of hostilities and the sustained presence of non-state armed groups in a cross-border territory. Armed actors seek to exert territorial control on both sides of the border, so it is not limited to only one of the states involved. (Vité 2009; ICRC 2011) This new conflict dynamic is aggravated by the lack of diplomatic relations between Colombia and Venezuela, which were severed in 2019 (BBC News 13/02/2019; ICG 30/04/2021; Infobae 03/01/2022).

risk_title: Reduced income from agricultural livelihoods and rising food prices result in reduced access to food for (mainly) socioeconomically vulnerable groups.
risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
trigger:
-  Unforeseen heavy rains continue to cause flooding in northeast and southern Brazil.
- Crop loss and poor harvests
- Income reduction
- Higher food price increases
- Continued mobility limitations due to road destruction​
- Reduced government revenue​.
- Decreasing exports
vulnerability: The number of people affected is calculated using the average population by vulnerable groups that can be calculated. There are figures for the number of people in poverty, Venezuelan migrants and indigenous people. The number of peasants is not clear.
rationale: The impact of climate events in Brazil will increase the number of food insecure people. This risk is focused on the overall picture in Brazil, but mainly affects the most vulnerable populations: indigenous communities, Venezuelan migrants, people living in poverty and farmers. Within these groups, women and children represent a population most likely to suffer from food insecurity

risk_title: A reduction in subsidies and the suspension of foreign financial aid result in severe electricity and fuel shortages, leading to crop failures, loss of livelihoods, and worsening food insecurity.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
-Further increase in fuel and electricity prices as part of economic reforms.
-Further cut in foreign aid.
-Increase of electricity consumption because of high temperature in summer.
-Power cuts affecting the functioning of hospitals and other health facilities.
-Tribes in northern Sudan and Port Sudan disrupting fuel and electricity.
vulnerability: People have been dealing with humanitarian crises for a long time, and their coping capacities are about to be exhausted. There is a good presence of humanitarian organisations that may reduce the severity of the impact.
rationale:
Sudan has been following a new economic three-year reform program with the International Monetary Fund since June 2021, which requires reducing subsidies on prices of electricity and fuel (IMF accessed on 15/02/2022). In January 2022, the government announced increasing prices of electricity by more than 460%, mostly affecting the agriculture sector (Reuters 24/01/2022). In February, fuel prices increased by nearly 13% above a 400% spike in October 2020 (Reuters 05/02/2022 ; Dabanga 28/10/2020). Further cuts are likely throughout 2022, especially as global fuel prices are increasing because of the Russia-Ukraine conflict (3ayin 05/02/2022). Sudan is at risk of further cuts in foreign aid, following suspension of financial aid from several countries after the military takeover in October (Reuters 08/12/2021).  
The increase in electricity prices have already affected northern Sudan farmers, who depend on electricity to irrigate crops. The fear of the wheat crop failure led the farmers to protest and block Shiryan El-Shamal highway (linking Egypt to Sudan) between 9 January-16 February, demanding freezing the increase in electricity prices (Dabanga 10/01/2022). Despite the government exempting the agriculture sector from the increase until 30 April, similar blockade events will likely re-escalate in May (Dabanga 17/02/2022). Farmers will likely pressure the government by disrupting the electrical supply line from Meroe dam in northern Sudan (Dabanga 14/01/2022). The dam contributes to Sudan’s electricity production, and disruptions will likely result in severe shortages in electricity across the country where already power cuts occur every three to four days (Al Jazeera 05/01/2022).  
Increase of fuel and electricity prices will likely reignite the Beja tribe's blockade of Port Sudan. The Beja tribe will likely close the pipeline that carries oil from South Sudan to Khartoum and create severe shortages in fuel, like the blockade that took place in mid-September, objecting a failed military coup attempt. (Dabanga 27/09/2021). 

Risk update: The risk has partially materialised. Expected increases in fuel prices have affected agriculture, contributing to a price spike for some food items and worsening food security levels. There has, however, been no escalation of tensions between the Government and farmers in northern Sudan and no disruption to the electrical supply line from Merowe dam. Electricity did not see further cuts in subsidies, meaning no further increases in electricity prices, unlike for fuel. At the beginning of August, transportation costs increased by 40–50% following an increase in petrol and diesel prices in the country. High fuel prices have affected agricultural activities, such as land preparation, which usually starts in April. The removal of fuel and electricity subsidies in late 2021 also increased the prices of some food items like sorghum and wheat in 2022. Sorghum prices in July were more than 600% higher than in the same month in 2021.

risk_title: Continued COVID-19 movement restrictions and extreme weather conditions during the cyclone season will likely delay the recovery process after the tsunami and result in increased humanitarian needs.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
Increase in COVID-19 cases.
Lockdown measures extended.
Increase access constraint on NGOs
Delays in repairing infrastructure
vulnerability: Although a high number of people are expected to be affected, the presence of services and humanitarian organisations, as well as national preparedness mechanisms, lower the severity of impact.
rationale:
Tonga was impacted on 15 January by a volcanic eruption and a tsunami, which affected 80% of the population (84,000 people) (OCHA 19/01/2022). With relief aid coming from foreign countries into the island, COVID-19 cases started to be reported on 1 February. Previously, Tonga has only recorded one COVID-19 case since the start of the pandemic and the government has been applying strict measures on international travel to avoid an outbreak (TIME 03/02/2022).  
A total of 355 cases have been confirmed between 1-26 February (WHO accessed on 27/02/2022 ; Matangy 27/02/2022).  Despite a relatively high vaccination rate (60%) in Tonga, the government fears that a COVID-19 outbreak can be a bigger threat to the country than the volcanic eruption (The Guardian 02/02/2022). This fear, in addition to the rapid increase in cases, has led the government to impose a nationwide lockdown on 2 February that will likely create delays in the recovery process and prolong people’s suffering following the volcanic eruption. Lockdowns in Tonga mean that people need to stay indoors, internal travelling between Tonga’s islands is suspended, schools and non-essential businesses are closed, and foreign nationals are not allowed into the country (Crisis24 01/02/2022 ; Al Jazeera 02/02/2022). Despite easing restrictions on 28 February, primary and high schools continue home schooling and nighttime curfew is still active between 8:00pm to 5:00am (Matangy 27/02/2022). 
The cyclone season affects Tonga between January-March (Govt. Tonga 14/10/2021). If a weather disturbance impacts the island during this season, combined with COVID-19 movement restrictions, the repairing of infrastructure, specifically roads damaged by the tsunami, will likely be further delayed. Access constraints facing humanitarian organizations will likely increase because of potential floods, movement restrictions, and the damage to infrastructure, hindering the delivery of aid (OCHA 10/02/2022 ; Crisis24 07/02/2022).

risk_title: Social and political instability because of the deteriorating economic situation and tensions around the parliamentary elections result in increased humanitarian needs.
risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
vulnerability: Rural livelihoods are under a lot of pressure due to the consecutive poor rainfall seasons and high prices of inputs, forcing households to engage in negative coping strategies that may be detrimental to their health and the environment
rationale:
The socio-economic situation in Zimbabwe is affecting access to education for 4.6 million children. Since 7 February, teachers organised a nationwide strike to demand an increase in salaries from 100-500 dollars per month. To stop the strike, the government is threatening 90% of public school students of suspension. If the government suspend teacher, the likelihood of violent demonstrations and clashes with security forces will increase. 

Meanwhile, the parliamentary elections scheduled on 26 March are finalized. Zimbabwe’s leading opposition party won the majority of the parliamentary seats (19 out of the 28) on the elections on 26 March. But the ruling party still holds the majority of overall seats, as they have won 145 seats from the 210 available seats in parliament in 2018.  Prior to the election, one person died and others were injured in clashes at an opposition party rally in between 26-27 February. The country’s main opposition leader claimed his followers were attacked by ruling party supporters armed with machetes, spears and rocks.

There are already 7 million people requiring humanitarian assistance because of climatic shocks and a deteriorating economic environment, including the impact of COVID-19 pandemic. An escalation of violence related to the teachers’ strike and the parliamentary elections will likely result in social and political instability, increasing humanitarian needs, especially education.

risk_title: Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan’s strengthened presence in the newly merged tribal districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa increases humanitarian needs, protection concerns, and access constraints in the area.
vulnerability:
1) Given TTP’s aim to implement a particularly strict interpretation of Sharia law over the region, protection needs for women, girls, and youth are likely to increase
2) KP is home to many of the most food insecure Pakistanis living in geographically remote locations with poor infrastructure, limited logistics, and significant insecurity
rationale:
US-Taliban peace deal in early 2020, precipitated a resurgence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) activity in Pakistan which has been further boosted by Taliban’s takeover in Afghanistan, with whom the TTP has a longstanding relationship (USIP 19/01/2022, Diplomat 06/01/2022, RF/ERL 13/01/2022). Since then, TTP incidents have increased rising to 122% in 2021 compared to 2020 and reversing the decreasing trend in the last five years (ACLED accessed on 14/02/2022, PIPS 01/2022). Pakistani military personnel in the newly merged tribal districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan province received most of the attacks (PICSS 01/01/2022).  
The TTP capacity has increased, as the Taliban leadership released imprisoned senior TTP commanders and a number of fighters, granting them de facto political sanctuary and movement’s freedom in and operation from Afghanistan. The TTP has acquired modern weapons and expanded their recruitment and presence in Pakistan, inside and beyond the newly merged districts of KP, and their financial resources - from extortion, smuggling, and taxes – have grown dramatically (VOA News 09/01/2022, RF/ERL 18/05/2021).  
The TTP leadership have a natural affinity towards the Taliban, even claiming to be a branch of the Taliban in Pakistan, yet they also retain good relations with the Islamic State in the Khorasan Province (ISKP). While Pakistan’s prime minister and multiple senior politicians publicly welcomed the Taliban’s takeover, the Taliban have shown no indication that they will prevent the TTP from operating from Afghanistan. Although, TTP initially rejected offers of dialogue from the Pakistan government, the negotiations did start in Nov 2022. The ceasefire has since failed but negotiations are reported to continue (Carnegie 21/1202/2022, RF/ERL 13/01/2022, RF/ERL 18/05/2021, RF/ERL 24/01/2022). Stalled Taliban-mediated peace talks is likely to step up counter-insurgency operations which will grow TTP leverage and pressure to accept their provisions. This is likely to give greater concessions to TTP and reaffirm their legitimacy, which is highly likely to increase the humanitarian needs, protection concerns and human rights violations in the region. 
Violence against civilians and armed clashes in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces increased by 35% in July 2022 compared to the same time last year according to ACCLED, however it is overall not exclusive to TTP.
This risk has partially materialised considering the increased TTP influence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, widespread extortions, and heightened protection concerns for the local population (USIP 21/06/2022; Gandhara 17/08/2022; Gandhara 21/09/2022). 
The indefinite ceasefire between TTP and the government of Pakistan ended in September after TTP accused the government of breaching it.

risk_title: A higher presence of non-Ukrainian and non-Russian fighters in Ukraine forming paramilitary groups increases security incidents and instability, leading to increased displacement and a worsened humanitarian situation.
vulnerability: The coping capacity of those affected would be limited because of the impact of current conflict and severe humanitarian access constraints
rationale:
The security situation in Ukraine have deteriorated significantly after the Russian military offensive started on 24 February 2022. Other non-Ukrainian and non-Russian have been participated in the conflict such as Chechens, Wagner, International legion and volunteers. This raise a risk of forming armed and terrorist groups because of the instability in the country. The risk is aggravated by the imported weaponry to the country. 
In the event of materializing the risk, the humanitarian situation is very likely to be severely impacted. Increasing civilian causalities and displacements is expected because of the expected increase in security incidents and instability. Humanitarian access is likely to be extremely constrained in various areas in the country.

Update: as at end of February 2023, there are no increase in paramilitary groups or terrorist attacks

risk_title: The withdrawal of the Barkhane force, as well as consequent increase in armed group clashes and territorial expansion, results in displacement, protection concerns, and the deterioration of humanitarian access.
trigger: Military coup; deterioration of relations between Mali and France;
vulnerability: The food insecurity outlook, which forecasts more than 1,800,000 people in need of emergency food assistance in June-August 2022, including 1,074,000 in Segou and Mopti regions only, could worsen under the cumulative effects of clashes and Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) economic sanctions. Agricultural inputs due to the disruption of the supply chain, people’s access to the fields will be even more difficult in case of attacks against civilians while agriculture is one of the main sources of income for the population.
rationale: This risk has materialised. Since the announcement of the withdrawal of the Barkhane force from Mali in February 2022 and its actual withdrawal in August, non-state armed groups have continued to expand their presence and activity across the country. The presence of non-state armed groups had already been affecting the north and centre of Mali; the humanitarian situation has also since started deteriorating in the south. After a few rare incursions, the activity of armed groups in the south of the country is intensifying, closing several schools particularly in the regions of Sikasso and Koulikoro. Despite the junta promising to foster the effectiveness and response of the Malian army − with support from the Russian paramilitary company Wagner − after the departure of the Barkhane force, attacks targeting civilians and troops have multiplied across the country. Abuses against civilians by the Malian security forces and the paramilitary group Wagner are also reported. The attacks are getting closer to the capital Bamako. One of these attacks targeted the Kati military camp on 22 July, where the leader of the junta was living. This attack indicates a desire by the non-state armed groups to increase their activity in areas where they were previously not significantly active or present. The number of displaced people has grown in the regions of Bamako, Kayes, Koulikoro, and Sikasso as a result of the surge in attacks. The total number of displaced people across the country had risen from around 362,000 in February to over 396,000 as at 31 July.

risk_title: The Russian recognition of Transnistria, the separatist region in Moldova, leads to increasing security incidents and displacements.
trigger:
1. Russian - Ukrainian conflict.
2. The existence of Russian peacekeeping forces in this region.
rationale:
In 1992 pro-Russian separatists in the region of Transnistria took control and announced their independence on Moldova. The Russian peacekeeping forces are present in this region which is very close to the Ukrainian borders.
Due to the insecurity in Ukraine because of the Ukrainian-Russian conflict and the Russian military in various Ukrainian cities, there are concerns on Russian recognition of this region leading to increasing security incidents and displacements in Transnistria.

Although it remains a probability and should be monitored, this risk has not materialised despite the Russian full-scale invasion being a potential trigger.

risk_title: Access to quality public services and increasing prices in Poland as a result of displacements from Ukraine affect both the displaced population and hosting communities.
trigger: Russian - Ukrainian conflict
vulnerability: Displaced people and host communities are very likely to be most affected.
rationale:
There were around 2.5 million refugees from Ukraine displaced into Poland by early April 2022. At the time, it was assumed by ACAPS analysts that the number of refugees would increase rapidly because of the ongoing hostilities in Ukraine, and that the high number of refugees would add extra pressure on the Polish infrastructure such as transportation and access to basic services, including medical facilities and schools. Prices are likely to increase, in particular, housing and rent costs, and in turn affect poorer households in the country (including both refugees and the host community).  

This risk has partially materialised. Firstly, The number of refugees did not increase, but rather decreased. As at early February 2023, there are around 1.5 million refugees from Ukraine in Poland. The high number of new refugees from Ukraine did add extra pressure on the health care and education systems in Poland, but not really on transportation. The waiting time for an average health service increased from 3.4 months to 3.6 months between Nov 2021 and Nov 2022. There is insufficient availability of places in schools and kindergartens for refugee children. The cost of housing and rent did spike because of the sudden increase in demand for housing, and the availability of apartments decreased.  For example, Average price of a studio (up to 38 sqm) rose by 33% in Warsaw, by 40% in Gdańsk, by 42% in Wrocław and by 44% in Kraków year to year (some of the largest cities).

risk_title: The disruption of the global supply chain following the Russian invasion of Ukraine disrupt food availability and increase food insecurity in Lebanon and Syria.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
- Increased prices of bread and other main food items (in both countries)
- Deeper socioeconomic crisis (in both countries)
- Increased violence and discrimination against Syrian refugees and other minorities
-Returns of refugees from Lebanon to Syria 
- Drought conditions in Syria
- reliance (of both countries) on wheat imports, amongst other staples, from Russia and Ukraine
- increased poverty levels in Lebanon
vulnerability: Years of conflict, political tensions, and displacement as a result of 10 years of war in Syria and the socioeconomic crisis in Lebanon since 2019 have deepened or generated humanitarian needs in both countries. In Lebanon the most economically vulnerable and the displaced population would be the most impacted by the risk
rationale:
Following the beginning of Russia military offensive on Ukraine, on 24 February, the international community responded with a number of sanctions, including those affecting trade to/from Russia. Ukraine industry and agriculture activities have been suspended due to the ongoing war. Russia and Ukraine together account for 29% of the world's wheat supply. Russia halted their grain exports to protect their own supply and Ukraine trade flows remains difficult and unclear because of conflict. Both Lebanon and Syria import wheat from Russia. This has increased the threat of food insecurity for the countries that depend on Russian and Ukraine for what imports- including the Middle East (and put pressure on other producers, as they need to make sure they have enough stocked to feed the population). The energy market has been impacted as well – and did not recover completely from the COVID-19 impact on the economy - and it is likely take its toll on the economies and prices, resulting in higher costs of fuel and gas. Higher costs of fuel will likely push the cost of basic goods even higher. About 52% of Lebanon wheat imports comes from Russia and 15% from Ukraine. While, 24% of Syria wheat procurement is originated from Russia. Both countries are struggling with food insecurity rates and deepened economic crisis. 
Lebanon is experiencing a socioeconomic crisis in addition to the hosting high numbers of Syrian refugees. Almost 90% of the Syrian refugee population lives at income levels below the Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket, and 80% of Lebanese were pushed to live in multidimensional poverty in 2021. In 2021, 50% the Syrian refugee population and 22% of Lebanese households were food insecure – and it might get worse. 
Syria remains in in emergency driven by more than ten years of violence, hostilities and protracted displacement. About 12.4 million Syrian are food insecure, with another 1.3 million are severely food insecure in Syria. Food prices are higher than a year ago: the cost of a WFP food basket is 86% higher in January 2021 than it was a year ago. 14.6 million people in Syria are in need of humanitarian assistance, including approximately 5 million people classified as experiencing extreme or catastrophic levels of humanitarian need. 
The situation in both, Syria and Lebanon, might deteriorate and significant number of people who are already face food insecurity might face higher levels of food insecurity, while others previously not food insecure might fall into it.  In addition, higher costs of basic goods will reduce households’ purchasing power. This is likely to increase people's adoption of negative coping mechanisms. With increased prices and disruption of the supply chain also the procurement and operations of humanitarian organisations could be affected. 
Some families in Lebanon are spending up to 50% of their monthly income on bread. The Lebanese pound has lost 90% of its value since 2019, resulting in unsustainable governmental subsidies for bread. Bread prices have increased more than fourfold since last year. The situation is compounded because of the repercussions from the Beirut port explosion; Lebanon’s import capacity has decreased by 60%, and damage caused by the port explosion reduced grain storage capacity by 100,000 metric tons. By August 2022, there are increased reports of Bread shortages and long queues for bread at bakeries are increasing violence against Syrian refugees.
In Syria, wheat production in 2022 is 75% less than pre-crisis production levels, because of a combination of dry weather conditions, conflict damages to the irrigation system, and a deteriorated economy due to the protracted crisis that has resulted in the devaluation of the Syrian pound, and in trun, increased prices of fuel and agricultural inputs. 
Despite the UN facilitated grain deal in late July allowing security guarantees by Russia for Ukraine to export wheat and stabilise global food prices, there remains a risk that Russia may still withdraw from the deal to apply political pressure in support of its invasion.

UPDATE: the risk has materialised but mainly due to compounding risks and deteriorating socio-economic trends and not exclusively because of disruptions of imports

risk_title: Ukrainians fleeing the war face human trafficking and protection concerns when displacing within the country and internationally because of the presence of smuggling and human trafficking networks
country: Poland; Ukraine; Slovakia; Romania; Moldova; Hungary; Austria; Portugal; Germany; Sweden; France; Slovenia; Spain; Czech Republic; Netherlands; Israel; Monaco; United Arab Emirates; Russia
iso3: POL; UKR; SVK; ROU; MDA; HUN; AUT; PRT; DEU; SWE; FRA; SVN; ESP; CZE; NLD; ISR; MCO; ARE; RUS
trigger:
Russian - Ukrainian conflict
Presence of human trafficking networks
vulnerability:
Women and children are very likely to be most affected. 
The coping capacity is supports to Poland.

Update 4 April 2023:
The particularly vulnerable groups are: Women, girls, children, people not eligible to or not able to access Temporary Protection, the elderly, LGBT, Roma, as well as survivors of domestic violence.

People who experience acute economic needs, are cut off from support networks, or reach incomplete or false information during travel are particularly exposed to forced labour and sex trafficking. 

Coping capacity of EU countries is assessed relatively positively by UNODC, whereas LaStrada & the Freedom Fund point to gaps in the anti-trafficking response, including limited governments' capacity to adopt anti-trafficking measures proportionate to the scale of the crisis, uncoordinated information, insufficient response coordination and other.
rationale:
Conflict re-escalation in Ukraine since 24 February 2022 has forced over 6 million people to leave their homes and seek safety in neighbouring countries, including Poland, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, Moldova, and Russia. Russia does not fully meet the minimum international requirements to end human trafficking and Ukrainians forcibly displaced into Russia are particularly vulnerable to trafficking.

Additionally, almost 6 million people were estimated to be internally displaced, with 3.6 million still displaced in early 2024. Human traffickers have in the past targeted IDPs in the Russian controlled areas in Ukraine, and subjected some to forced labor, forced conscription, and sexual exploitation including through kidnapping and torture. This likely worsened after the full-scale Russian invasion and consequent increased number of displacements.

Human trafficking and protection risks are a significant concern during the time of displacements. Women and children are the vast majority of displaced people and can be exposed to abduction, detention, lack of access to services, sexual abuse, forced labour, and torture.

Incidents of human trafficking of Ukrainian refugees and displaced people continue to be reported. Suspected human trafficking cases have been investigated or recorded in the EU, with suspected cases included trafficking in people for sexual exploitation, labour exploitation and illegal surrogacy. There were also human trafficking cases investigated in Ukraine.

The 2022 Global report on trafficking in persons estimated that the share of Ukrainian victims among all detected victims of human trafficking in the EU would rise. ILO acknowledges the risk of human trafficking and has been implementing awareness raising measures among IDPs in Ukraine, refugees in Moldova, employers and employment services. 1 in 100 female refugees from Ukraine received proposals to work in the sex industry, 1 in 50 received requests for sexual favours and 1 in 500 suffered sexual violence. 

Incidents of forced labour and forced conscriptions continue to be reported in the Russian controlled areas in Ukraine since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022.

risk_title: Food insecurity escalates as a result of natural disasters, territorial control by criminal gangs, rising prices, and declining imports. The most affected population is children under the age of five. Gang violence affects the health, sanitation care, and food aid of this population.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
- Natural disasters, territorial control by gangs, rising prices and declining imports could increase food insecurity in Haiti. 
- The war in Ukraine could be a trigger for higher prices and reduced imports. 
- Haiti is mainly dependent on imports, so a decrease in imports reduces food access, availability and stability.
vulnerability: The food crisis already underway in Haiti has been one of the main focuses of the work of humanitarian organisations and governments in other countries. Ongoing natural disasters affect harvests and reduce food stability. The limited access to humanitarian aid and the decrease in imports makes it difficult to address this crisis, increases prices, decreases access and availability of food.
rationale:
The impact of continuing natural disasters, increased territorial control by gangs, rising prices and declining imports will increase the number of food insecure people in Haiti. Between March and June these conditions could increase the number of hungry people to 4.5 million, of which 1.3 million would be in IPC Phase 4. 
The war in Ukraine could be a trigger for higher prices and reduced imports. Haiti is mainly dependent on food imports, so its decline will increase the number of food insecure people to 4.6 million after June. Approximately 20 per cent of children under the age of five in Cité Soleil are suffering from severe or moderate acute malnutrition, five percentage points above the emergency threshold. If violence continues, these figures may continue to grow.

risk_title: Non-adherence to the 2018 peace agreement and clashes between the SPLM/A-IO and SSPDF forces throughout South Sudan lead to displacement, increased humanitarian needs, and increased humanitarian access constraints.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
trigger:
-Attacks initiated by SSPDF on SPLM/A-IO in Unity and Upper Nile States in March 2022
-Withdrawal of SPLM/A-IO from talks to form unified security forces in accordance with the 2018 peace agreement
-Temporary deployment of security forces to First Vice President Riek Machar's residence in Juba from 26 to 28 March
vulnerability: The South Sudanese population has high pre-existing vulnerabilities due to the impact of years of conflict, high poverty rates, inadequate access to social services and seasonal flooding.
rationale:
There is a possibility that the 2018 peace agreement could collapse due to renewed hostilities between principal signatories. This is after the SPLM/A-IO (South Sudan People's Liberation Movement/Army-In Opposition), a principal signatory to the peace deal, declared it had pulled out from talks to form a unified national army, following repeated military attacks by SSPDF forces on the group’s military bases in parts of Upper Nile state.
Tension between the peace deal signatories escalated, with security forces also deployed to cordon off First Vice-President Riek Machar's residence in Juba from 26 to 28 March. 
Humanitarian impact: increased levels of internal/ international displacement and elevated humanitarian needs across all sectors for the 8.3 million people currently in need. 
This risk did not materialize. After mediation by various regional bodies, including IGAD and the AU, tensions were de-escalated and both parties agreed to form a unified army.

risk_title: The depletion of foreign currency reserves and economic decline affect people's access to basic goods and services and livelihoods, leading to humanitarian needs among the most vulnerable.
trigger:
- If the government does not restructure its debt repayment scheme, the economic crisis will continue.

- The economic crisis will continue to affect availability of basic goods.

- Shortages and increasing prices of basic goods have already resulted in reduced access to food, fuel, electricity, medicines, basic services, and livelihoods, including those that rely on tourism. 

-  Lack of access to basic goods, livelihoods, and basic services develop the needs into humanitarian needs for the most vulnerable groups.
vulnerability: poverty-affected (vulnerable) groups, particularly the elderly and those living in rural areas
rationale:
Sri Lanka foreign currency reserves are down by 70% since January 2020 at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.  Sri Lanka’s economic crisis started even before the pandemic, and in March 2022 has already resulted in an acute shortage of essential supplies like food, medicine, milk powder, cooking gas and fuel, and a secondary impact lack of electricity. Current foreign currency reserves as at late March 2022 can cover the national demand of basic goods enough for about a month only. Sri Lanka is getting loans from with India and China to solve current crisis, and is in talks with IMF, however Sri Lanka's debt cycle is unsustainable, and requires restructuring, otherwise, Sri Lanka risks developing a humanitarian crisis.

On 1 April, protestors tried to storm the presidential residence. The president declared a state of emergency and a curfew for 36 hours. On 4 April, all the ministers submitted letters of resignation.

OCHA has pointed out that 5.7 million people are in need in June 2022.

risk_title: The impact of the war in Ukraine on global food and oil prices contributes to a worsening economy and social instability in Egypt, leading to police response to increased demonstrations.
trigger:
Russian - Ukrainian conflict
Depreciation of the Egyptian pound
Reduced purchasing power
Arbitrary detention of demonstrators
vulnerability: People have medium coping capacity in Egypt since there is no active conflict affecting people or a severe food insecurity crisis.
rationale:
The impact of the war in Ukraine on Egypt’s economy will likely cause further depreciation of the Egyptian pound, reduce purchasing power, and trigger social instability and demonstrations.

The war in Ukraine and the global increase of prices of grains and fuel contributed to worsening the economic situation in Egypt and increased government spending. Meanwhile, revenues from tourism were affected because Ukrainians and Russians are among the most nationalities of tourists in Egypt. Egypt had to seek financial support from the IMF, which it had obtained in October. Following the agreement with the IMF, the Egyptian pound depreciated by 14.5% against the US dollar and interest rates were raised by 200 points on 27 October. People have called for mass protests on 11 November over worsening economic conditions. The Egyptian authorities detained dozens of people who called for demonstrations, particularly in Cairo and Giza, which will likely increase the likelihood of social instability in the country. 
As at December 2023, inflation rates are still high, despite showing a slight improvement in November and December. However, there has been no social tensions or clashes with police forces reported due to the impact of the war in Ukraine. 

Context: Russia and Ukraine are major countries producing and exporting cereals and vegetable oils. The Ukraine crisis is causing an increase of food and energy prices and putting additional people at risk of food insecurity over the next six months. Over 69% of the wheat in Egypt comes from Russia and Ukraine, the conflict led to block shipments from the Black Sea or disrupted the agriculture process. The government announced boundaries for the bread prices due to increasing its prices.

risk_title: Drought across Morocco leads to water shortages, decreased agriculture production, and increased food and vegetable prices
trigger: Drought
vulnerability: Farmers and people under the poverty line are vulnerable to agricultural disruptions and increased commodity prices.
rationale: In 2022, Morocco faced the most acute drought in 40 years because of climate change. The country received little rain that year, 64% less than the standard, and authorities announced reserving only 11% of what they would save in an average year. The most affected cities were Marrakesh and Oujda. The Government supported the agricultural sector with EUR 1 billion (over USD 1 billion) to address the problem. In Morocco, agriculture is the biggest employer, accounting for 17% of output in 2021.

risk_title: As a response to Spain changing its positions towards Western Sahara, more departures to Europe departing from Algeria are possible, increasing the protection risks for migrants on the move.
trigger: Spain had changed its position towards the Western Sahara conflict to side with Morocco.
vulnerability: Protection risks for migrants crossing at sea
rationale: On March 2022, Spain had changed her policy for Western Sahara conflict to side with Morocco. Spain receives about 40 percent of its gas from Algeria that could be at risk. Although, Algeria seen as unlikely to use gas as pressure point in Spain. More departures could be allowed from Algeria without proper checks. Migrants attempting to cross to Europe by sea are often face protection related risks and lack of safety during the journey. Need for multi-sectoral assistance is also expected upon arrival.

risk_title: Electoral violence throughout Nigeria results in protection concerns
trigger:
- 2022–2023 election season
- Past episodes of electoral violence in the country
- Hate speech around the elections/candidates
vulnerability: The population of northern Nigeria has higher poverty rates and lower literacy levels compared to other regions in the country, leading to vulnerability.
rationale: Electoral violence has featured in most Nigerian elections since 1999, keeping the period between campaigns till elections highly volatile. During the September 2022 to March 2023 electoral period, some influential leaders started engaging in hate speech, leading to tensions and the possibility of violence and human rights violation, including extrajudicial killings by armed forces and groups. In the 12 months leading up to the elections held in February and March, ACLED recorded at least 200 violent incidents involving party members and supporters, resulting in nearly 100 fatalities. Unarmed civilians were the most targeted group. The risk of violence was higher in Rivers and Kano states, which had strategic electoral significance.

risk_title: Russian interference escalating violence in Moldova results in security concerns and disrupts access to services and humanitarian aid
trigger:
- Regional tensions following the Russian invasion of Ukraine
- Increasing protests by Sor (pro-Russian) political party
- Flare up of clashes between Moldova and Transnistria
vulnerability: Displaced people and host communities are very likely to be most affected. Owners of small business and unemployed youth will likely be affected by additional impacts on economy.
rationale:
Anti-government protests attended by thousands of people began in Moldova in September 2022 and continued into early 2023. The protests were organised by the Sor (pro-Russia) political party, allegedly with funding from Russia. Russia likely aims to further the social tensions and political instability in Moldova. It is likely that attacks led by pro-Russian, including from Transnistria, will lead to flare up of clashes and increase humanitarian needs. The armed conflict in 1992 had led to the deaths of hundreds of people and the displacement of tens of thousands before reaching a ceasefire.

The protests are happening in a period of socio-economic distress for the country. This was caused by the negative economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the effects of 2020 drought, and the Russian full-scale invasion in Ukraine, including the refugee influx in 2022. These have been compounded by an energy crisis, after a 30% reduction of gas supply by Russia in October 2022, which reached 50% by end of 2022. Energy costs are affecting poor households, particularly those in rural areas. The inflation rate in December 2022 reached 30%, up from 14% during the same period in 2021. Both the Moldovan and refugee populations have been affected by economic hardship and became more reliant on governmental and international support. Ukrainian refugees
continue to arrive in the country, with almost 110,000 present as at mid-March 2023, up from 90,000 in October 2022.

Update: despite Russian attempts to destabilize Moldova, this risk has not materialised in 2023, however factors such as ongoing Russian military presence in the Moldovan Transistria region, and continued Russian interference in Moldova remain relevant in the future, particularly as Moldova achieved open accession negotiations with EU in December 2023, and will be holding presidential elections in late 2024. Russian interference in Moldova's internal politics continued into late 2024, however, the risk of significant violence remained unmaterialised.

risk_title: The expansion of armed groups from central Sahel to coastal countries (Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo) leads to displacement and increased food insecurity.
trigger: Advance of armed groups from the Sahel to the south, multiplication of attacks by armed groups in the Gulf of Guinea countries
vulnerability: The violence would mainly affect rural populations who live mainly from herding and agriculture. Thousands of people would lose their livelihoods.
rationale:
This risk is materialising at a slow pace. A progressive deterioration of the security situation in the northern regions of West African coastal countries is observed. Between October 2022 and January 2023, more than 73 violent incidents involving mostly non-state armed groups have been reported in the northern regions of Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo. On the same period in 2022, around 30 incidents were reported. These incidents included attacks on civilians and security forces, kidnappings, the destruction of property, and the use of improvised explosive devices. Benin is the country recording the highest number of attacks by armed groups, followed by Togo. In Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, the attacks are on a smaller scale given a still-low presence of armed groups, but these are becoming more regular.

risk_title: Possible social unrest following elections in university students’ associations causes delays in recovery after the cyclone season and further deteriorates food insecurity levels and increase humanitarian access constraints.
trigger:
1. Violence after elections of university students’ association.
